newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-TEXAS UTILITIES PRIMED FOR DEREGULATION.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-TEXAS UTILITIES PRIMED FOR DEREGULATION.

text.p: Texas regulators are pressing local electric utilities to file rate cases in the coming year to prepare for deregulation of the statewide grid, the state Public Utility Commissioner said.

The regulatory agency expects to have Texas utilities on a "glide path" toward deregulation before the state legislature opens its biennial session beginning in January 1999, PUC Commissioner Pat Wood said in a recent interview.

"Either they'll do it voluntarily or we'll ask them to come in," Wood said of the pending rate cases, which are being used to set up schedules for recovering stranded costs and trimming rates ahead of expected deregulation statewide.
The Texas legislature this year adjourned without passing a hotly debated deregulation bill, shifting focus to the PUC and Wood, the 35-year old head of the regulatory agency.
A former Baker & Botts attorney, Wood was directly involved in interstate natural gas deregulation as a legal advisor to a U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commissioner.
The Texas PUC is holding hearings on a proposed seven-year transition to an open market in the service territory controlled by New Orleans-based Entergy Corp.
Commission staffers also are in "low-level discussions" on a possible filing with Houston Lighting and Power, the Houston Industries Inc electric and gas utility.

But analysts say Texas-New Mexico Power Co may have come up with the blueprint for opening the state's grid to competition. The company proposed a five-year transition begninning Jan. 1, 1998 that would trim residential rates six percent and commercial rates by three percent while freezing industrial rates.

Through accelerated depreciation and a cap on earnings, the Fort Worth, Texas-based company's utilities would recover an estimated $210.5 million in stranded costs. Another $60 million or so would be recovered in a transmission charge after the stranded costs are "trued up" at market value.
The remaining piece of the puzzle for regulators is a "date certain" or target date for opening up the Texas grid.
While waiting for that decision from the legislature, Wood said stranded costs for the Texas utilities will be recovered gradually without raising rates.
"I do not think we need to be recovering costs faster than a straight, hard rate freeze would do," he said.
